title: Ekalavya and the teacher's fee
hookLine: a boy learns archery from a clay teacher, then pays with his thumb
carry: a guru removes darkness: look at the light
tomorrow: an old text pictures a line of blind people. who's at the front?
last: OFFERED WITH LOVE, RETURNED AS GRACE.

cards: Marketing guru. Fitness guru. Money guru.
The word turns up all over the feed, stuck to anyone with a following. Then there's the older kind: a teacher with a soft voice and a calm smile, retreats that fill up, comments full of thanks.
Scroll a little further and some comments are full of warnings. Both sides use the same word. So, one question for today: what does guru actually mean, and how would anyone tell a real one?

teach.h: GU: DARKNESS. RU: WHAT REMOVES IT.
teach.b: In Hindu life the word carries real weight. A guru is a teacher, and one Upanishad plays on the sounds: gu is darkness, ru is what removes it.

Families honor teachers at home and on Guru Purnima, and some lineages treat the guru as a living doorway to God. But the tradition doesn't hide what can go wrong, and the Mahabharata tells it plainly.
Ekalavya, a forest chief's son, asks the great archery teacher Drona to take him on. Drona refuses.

So Ekalavya goes into the woods, shapes Drona out of clay, and practices before the image every day, until he shoots better than Drona's favorite student, Arjuna. Drona had promised Arjuna no one would surpass him.
So he finds Ekalavya and asks for his teacher's fee: the boy's right thumb. Ekalavya cuts it off and gives it, gladly.
Many readers, Hindus among them, have long felt the teacher was the one who failed: the student's devotion was real, and the guru used it. The honor is real, and so is the caution.

teach.h: MUNDAKA: LEARNED, AND STEADY IN BRAHMAN.
teach.b: So the Upanishads give a test: the Mundaka tells a seeker to find a teacher who knows the scriptures and stands steady in Brahman, in God.
Many teachers put it simply: a lamp is known by its light.

teach.h: A DIFFERENT PLACE FOR THE TEACHER.
teach.b: A neighbor tradition says something close. In the Gospel of Matthew, Jesus warns about false prophets: "Ye shall know them by their fruits."

teach.h: HONOR THE LAMP. LOOK AT THE LIGHT.
teach.b: And an honest difference: some Hindu lineages honor a living guru as a doorway to God, while in the same Gospel Jesus tells his followers, "one is your Master, even Christ; and all ye are brethren."

how: Hindus honor teachers in many ways, from touching a teacher's feet to Guru Purnima celebrations, and the tradition's own texts describe the marks of a genuine teacher.

s: guru just means an expert with a big following
in Hindu life it means a teacher; one Upanishad hears it as the remover of darkness.
warnings about gurus are a modern idea from outside the tradition
the Mahabharata itself tells how Drona took Ekalavya's thumb, and the old texts describe true teachers.
Matthew's Gospel also gives a test for teachers: by their fruits
both look past the voice and the following, to what a life produces.

games.q: your uncle's meditation teacher has a huge following and a well-known name. your uncle says that proves he's the real thing. what would today's texts look at instead?
o: the light he gives: what his teaching and his life actually produce.
the size of the crowd: people don't keep following a fake for long.
the well-known name: a big title in the right lineage settles it.
games.why: the Mundaka looks for a teacher learned and steady in Brahman, and many teachers add: a lamp is known by its light. Matthew's Gospel says it in its own words: by their fruits.

practice: Many Hindus honor a teacher with folded hands and a small bow, in person or in the heart.
Fold your hands and count on your fingers the people who brought you some light: a teacher, a grandparent, a coach, a friend who explained something hard. Give each one a slow bow of the head.
Then ask of each: what light did they actually give?

wordCard.voice: Modern gurus and their cautions: living teachers, honored deeply, and the old texts' own warnings about how to choose one.

orig.note: Sanskrit: guru, teacher; the Advaya Taraka Upanishad hears gu as darkness and ru as its remover.

carryVoice: Your line, from Ekalavya's story: a guru removes darkness, so look at the light. Day done.
